extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, students of literature, poets, and scholars of narrative theory
extracted.subtask_description: Classifying and interpreting recurring mythic and narrative patterns (cyclical symbols, mythoi, comic/tragic structures, character types) to analyze or produce literature. Focus on how symbolic cycles, cosmology, and typical dramatic functions shape poetic and dramatic meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven categories of cyclical images
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye enumerates seven categories of images seen as different forms of rotary or cyclical movement which underpin symbolic meaning in literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories map natural/ mythic realms to narrative symbolism and should be used to identify how images participate in larger cyclical patterns (see the listed seven types below for particulars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divine-world cycle (death and rebirth of a god)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the divine world the central process is the death and rebirth, or the disappearance and return, or the incarnation and withdrawal, of a god; the dying god is reborn as the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associate divine cycles with solar, seasonal, or vegetation cycles (sun-god, vegetation god, reincarnation traditions); note 'identical recurrence' as a key structural principle (contrast Eastern acceptance of reincarnation vs Western assumptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire-world / celestial cycles (sun, solstice, moon)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fire-world presents cyclical rhythms: the daily sun journey (death at night and return), the solstitial solar year (newborn light threatened by darkness), and the lunar cycle (old moon, interlunar cave, new moon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link solar cycles to motifs like Christmas; lunar three-day sequence to Easter resurrection symbolism. Use these celestial cycles to interpret temporal and light/dark imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-world cycles (waking/dreaming; life/death)
rubrics_metrics.description: The human world is midway between spiritual and animal and reflects duality: the imaginative cycle of waking and dreaming (opposite of solar) and the ordinary biological cycle of life and death (generic, not individual, rebirth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to analyze contrasts between innocence and experience, day/dream imagery, and the moral/psychic cycles of human protagonists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal-world pattern (truncated lives and nostos exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Animal lives typically suggest the tragic process of life cut off violently; peaceful full-span animal lives are rare and are thematically tied to nostos or full close of cyclical movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret abrupt deaths or sacrificed animal figures as emblematic of tragic interruption of cycles; exceptions (e.g., Odysseus' dog) signal thematic closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vegetable-world cycle (annual seasons embodied in divine figures)
rubrics_metrics.description: The vegetable world supplies the annual cycle of seasons often identified with a divine figure who dies in autumn and revives in spring; the divine figure may be male (Adonis) or female (Proserpine) with differing symbolic structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map seasonal/harvest imagery to fertility/death/revival myths; attend to gendered variations in symbolism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spenglerian/organic cycle of civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets (and critics) often assimilate civilized life to an organic cycle of growth, maturity, decline, death, and rebirth, producing themes of golden age, millennium, wheel of fortune, ubi sunt elegy, nostalgia, and meditations over ruins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this schema to read historical or societal decline narratives and nostalgia as manifestations of organic-cycle thinking in poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water-symbolism cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: Water-symbolism follows its own cycle: rains → springs → fountains/brooks/rivers → the sea or snow → return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret water images as staged phases (source → flow → ocean) and map them to life stages, temporal phases, or purification motifs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-phase cyclical symbolism (seasons, day, life, water)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cyclical symbols are usually divided into four main phases: the four seasons typify four periods of the day (morning, noon, evening, night), water-cycle aspects, life periods (youth, maturity, age, death), etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use four-phase mapping (and note examples: Keats' Endymion = phases 1–2; The Waste Land = phases 3–4) and recognize there is no cycle of air—wind/spirit imagery suggests unpredictability or crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cosmology/obsolete science as a poetic grammar
rubrics_metrics.description: Symmetrical cosmology and obsolete scientific schemata (three spirits, four humors, five elements, seven planets, zodiacal signs) function as a grammar of literary imagery rather than as science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Ptolemaic and occult correspondences as structural principles and symbolic frameworks; be wary of 'versified science' imposing non-poetic descriptive form unless handled with tact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two fundamental narrative movements: cyclical and dialectical
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two fundamental movements of narrative: a cyclical movement within the order of nature, and a dialectical movement from that order into the apocalyptic world above (upward) or, rarely, into the demonic below (downward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this binary to classify narrative dynamics: cyclical/romance vs dialectical/apocalyptic; the upward movement corresponds to comic resolution, downward to tragic movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four narrative pregeneric elements (mythoi)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four categories broader than ordinary genres — the romantic, the tragic, the comic, and the ironic or satiric — function as 'mythoi' or generic plots that structure literature across genres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize these mythoi as pregeneric structural expectations: labeling a work 'tragic' or 'comic' sets expectations about structure and mood but not necessarily form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposed and blending relations among mythoi
rubrics_metrics.description: The mythoi form two opposed pairs (tragedy vs comedy; romance vs irony), but they can blend: comedy may blend into satire or romance, romance may be comic or tragic, tragedy can range from high romance to bitter realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate texts for mixtures or gradations among mythoi rather than strict categorical placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic plot structure: movement from one society to another
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy typically moves from one kind of society to another: obstructing characters initially control society, but by the end a new society crystallizes around the hero — the point of resolution is anagnorisis/cognitio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the obstructing forces, the crystallization moment (often a party/wedding/banquet signaling resolution), and the audience communion at the end. The plot often includes twist devices enabling the hero's wish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obstacles/blocking characters and their social function
rubrics_metrics.description: Obstacles are usually parental or father‑surrogates (rivals, usurpers) whose power indicates a criticism of the society that allows them; comedy tends to convert or reconcile blocking characters rather than merely exclude them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read blocking characters as embodiments of social norms or corrupt power; note whether the comedy's ethical interest concentrates on these blocking figures (comedy of manners) or on discovery mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic devices of proof and discovery (pistis → gnosis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the Tractatus Coislinianus, comic proofs (means of bringing about the happier society) include oaths, compacts, witnesses, ordeals (basanoi), and laws — corresponding to pistis (opinion) and gnosis (proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the play/fiction for legal‑rhetorical devices (oaths, witnesses, compacts, ordeals, sham laws) that enable the cognitio/anagnorisis and resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two compositional emphases in comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy can develop either by emphasizing blocking characters (comedy of manners) or by emphasizing scenes of discovery and reconciliation (romantic comedy); ethical interest shifts accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing comedy, decide whether the focus will be on satirizing/deflating specific humors or on orchestrating plot devices that produce reconciliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of humor: repetition and ritual bondage
rubrics_metrics.description: The humor principle is unincremental repetition (ritual bondage); repetition overdone becomes comic (whereas in tragedy repetition often leads to catastrophe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize stock comic patterns (repetition of gag/obsession/habit) as legitimate sources of humor; in composition, repetition conditions audience reflexes and supports stock types (e.g., Falstaff, Mrs. Micawber).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency of comedy to include and convert
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy tends to include as many people as possible in its final society: blocking characters are often reconciled or converted, and parasites/scapegoats may be allowed into the festive resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret final reconciliations, pardons, or reintegrations as central comic ethos rather than simple punitive closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulation of plot and permissibility of metamorphosis
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic endings are generally achieved by a plot twist (cognitio) — unlikely conversions, miraculous transformations, and providential assistance are allowed and do not violate comic decorum; happy endings are 'desirable' rather than 'true.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept improbable contrivances as structurally permissible in comedy; judge their success by how well they realize the comic society rather than by psychological realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization as function of dramatic structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterization depends on function: what a character is follows from what he has to do in the play; stock types are necessary skeletons for consistent dramatic character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or creating characters, align traits with dramatic functions (blocking, trickster, hero, etc.) and use stock types productively rather than as crude stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical comic character taxonomy (alazon, eiron, bomolochoi, agroikos)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tractatus lists comic types: alazons (impostors), eirons (self-deprecators), buffoons/bomolochoi, and the churl/agroikos; these form two opposed pairs and polarize comic action and mood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to identify dramatic roles: alazon group centers on senex iratus/heavy father and impostors; eiron centers on understated hero/heroine and trickster schemers; buffoon and churl color mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the trickster/vice/architectus of comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A tricky slave, vice, or trickster (dolosus servus, gracioso, vice, Puck/Ariel) often functions as the 'architectus' of comic action, orchestrating disguise and plot manipulations and seeking a reward (e.g., freedom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the agent who engineers the cognitio and comic reconciliation; their motifs (disguise, metamorphosis, mischief) indicate the mechanics of the comic plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ternary form of the total mythos of comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The total mythos of comedy often has a ternary form: stable/ideal order (often a remembered golden age), disruption/intermediate inversion (Saturnalia), and restoration (final society), sometimes unified by a benevolent figure linking phases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map comedy onto a three-part ritual/psychological structure when analyzing plot arcs; note how middle inversion and the restoring figure function ritually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical resemblance to jurisprudence (pistis vs gnosis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rhetoric of comedy resembles jurisprudence: the dianoia of comedy divides into opinion (pistis) and proof (gnosis), with proof subdivided into legal-like forms (oaths, compacts, witnesses, ordeals, laws).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use legal-rhetorical analysis to track how comic actions convert social opinion into demonstrable proof within the plot's logic.
